q2: Every electronic circuit starts with three ideas: voltage (the pressure on the electrons), current (how many of them pass), and resistance (what holds the current back). Before we move on to boards, we'll understand these together and learn to read resistors from their colors.
q4: The basics — where do the electrons go?
q5: “Voltage is the pressure a battery puts on electrons to make them move through a wire, and current is how many electrons pass a point each second. Resistance holds that movement back; the higher the voltage or the lower the resistance, the larger the current. Ohm's law ties these three quantities together.”
q6:
Imagine you want to power a small lamp. The first thing you need is a battery; a battery works like a water pump that turns chemical energy into electrical pressure.

That pressure is “voltage”, and it sets the electrons moving in the wire. But be careful! If the current produced by this pressure gets too large, the lamp burns out.

This is where “resistance” comes to help; just like the narrowness of a pipe, resistance makes it harder for electrons to pass and controls the current.

Now it's your turn! By adjusting the current precisely, bring it to a level where the lamp lights up brightly without burning out.

q8: Use the slider to open the path little by little and watch how the electrons start to move.
q9: Open it enough for sufficient current to arrive and the LED to light.
q10: Be careful not to overdo it — very low resistance means very high current and a burnt LED!
q12: On the way — decoding a resistor's color bands
q13: In the 1920s radio engineers were fed up. Electronic parts had become so tiny that the numbers printed on them looked like faded dots. Worse, when a part was soldered onto a board, the number would turn to the back side and vanish! Repairmen had to hunt for the number with a flashlight like hunters. Until someone had an idea: “Why not use colors instead of numbers?”
q14: Every resistor has four color bands that encode its value: the first and second bands make the two digits of the number, the third band multiplies that number by a factor (a power of ten), and the fourth band shows the allowed error (tolerance). Now it's your turn to read and build this code by hand — the very 220-ohm resistor we'll put in front of the LED in the LED-lighting mission.

q22: A one-way valve for current — anode and cathode
q23: “A diode is like a one-way door: current passes through it in only one direction. An LED is a diode that also gives off light when current flows through it. Its longer leg is positive (the anode) and its shorter leg is negative (the cathode); if you connect it the other way round, no current passes and it won't light.”
q24:
LED stands for “light-emitting diode”. It has two legs: the anode (+), which is the longer leg, and the cathode (−), which is shorter and sits next to the flat edge of the body. The anode must face the battery's positive side. A resistor is also placed in the path so the current doesn't get too high and the LED doesn't burn out.

In the circuit below the LED is connected backwards and doesn't light. Fix its direction.

q26: Read the label next to the LED's legs: the long leg is the anode (+) and the short leg (the side with the flat edge of the body) is the cathode (−). Which one is connected to the battery's positive side?

q30: A small, fast battery — charging and discharging
q31: “A capacitor is like a small, very fast battery: when connected to a battery, electric charge gathers on its two plates (charging), and when connected to a load, it gives all of it back at once (discharging). A bigger capacitor holds more charge.”
q32:
A capacitor has two metal plates close together with an insulator between them. The battery pours charge onto the plates until the capacitor is full. Then if you disconnect it from the battery and connect it to an LED, the LED stays lit until the charge runs out and then slowly fades.

This is why circuits use capacitors to hold power for short moments and to smooth out voltage.
q33: Press the “Charge” button and watch the capacitor fill up gradually (faster at first, slower at the end).
q34: Wait until the capacitor is completely full.
q35: Now press “Discharge” to connect the capacitor to the LED.
q36: Watch the LED light up, then dim and go out as the capacitor empties; after that the mission completes automatically.
q38: An electronic switch — light 5 LEDs with a single pin
q39: “A transistor is like an electric switch: you put a very small current on the control leg (Base) and a much larger current flows from the collector to the emitter. A microcontroller pin only gives about 20 milliamps, so the transistor helps it control several LEDs or even a motor at once.”
q40:
Every ordinary LED draws about 20 milliamps (each with its own 220Ω resistor). A microcontroller pin also supplies only about 20 milliamps, which means just one LED directly. The simple BC547 transistor passes up to about 100 milliamps, which is exactly these 5 LEDs.

On the breadboard below the 5 LEDs are already in place (100 milliamps in total). In transistor mode: the Collector (C) leg connects to the LEDs, the Emitter (E) to the battery's negative, and the Base (B) to the pin through a 1kΩ resistor. First try directly from the pin, then with the transistor.
q41: First keep the “Directly from the pin” mode and turn the signal on; watch all 5 LEDs go very dim and the pin get hot.
q42: Now press “With transistor”; the BC547 sits on the breadboard: C to the LEDs, E to negative and B to the pin through a resistor.
q43: Watch all 5 LEDs light at full brightness, because the main current comes from the battery, not the pin; the pin only gives a few milliamps to the Base.
q44: When all 5 LEDs light up with the transistor, the mission completes automatically.
q46: Get a steady 5 V from a 9 V battery — and see where the heat comes from
q47: “Connecting a 9 V battery straight to a 5 V board burns it out. A regulator is a part that takes any voltage (within limits) and delivers a clean, constant one; like a pressure-reducing valve that holds the output at one value whatever pressure comes in.”
q48:
The 7805 linear regulator has three legs: input (IN), ground (GND) and output (OUT). Whatever voltage between roughly 7 and 35 volts you give the input, you get a steady 5 volts on the output. That's why many Arduino boards and projects run from a 9 V battery or a 12 V adapter. For the STM32's 3.3 V there is a similar part (such as the AMS1117-3.3).

A linear regulator “burns off” the extra voltage, meaning it turns it into heat: power wasted = (input voltage − output voltage) × current. The bigger the difference or the current, the hotter the part gets, and if it goes past a limit, the thermal protection cuts the output. Two small capacitors are also placed beside it so the output has no noise.
q49: First look: the battery is connected directly to the 5 V board and the board is burnt. Raise and lower the voltage and see that only a narrow range is safe.
q50: Press the “With 7805 regulator” button; now any input between 7 and 15 volts keeps the output at a steady 5 volts. As soon as you use the regulator, the mission completes.
q51: (Optional) Take the input below 7 volts: the regulator needs about 2 volts of headroom (dropout) and the output is no longer 5.
q52: (Optional) Raise the input and the load current until the regulator gets hot and the thermal protection shuts it off; power wasted = (Vin − Vout) × I.
q53: (Optional) Build a healthy case: input 7 to 10 volts, a steady 5 V output and a temperature under 100 degrees.
q55: 8 outputs with only 3 pins — clock, latch and a challenge
q56: “A shift register is like a queue: with every clock a new bit joins the queue and the rest move one step forward. When the queue is ready, you light all 8 outputs at once with LATCH; that is, 8 LEDs with only 3 Arduino pins.”
q57:
The 74HC595 is a “serial-to-parallel converter”: it takes bits in on a single wire and places them on 8 outputs at the same time; for an LED bar, a seven-segment display, an LED matrix and anywhere you've run out of pins.

The Arduino Uno has limited pins, but you want 8 LEDs. The 74HC595 chip gives you eight outputs (Q0 to Q7) with just three wires: DATA (the bit you send: 0 or 1), CLOCK (each pulse moves the bits one step forward) and LATCH (puts the ready contents on the outputs all at once).

Inside the chip there are two rows of eight cells: the shift row, in which bits step along with CLOCK, and the latch row, which the LEDs are connected to and which copies from the shift row only on LATCH. That's why the LEDs don't flicker while the bits are moving.

This mission has three stages: first CLOCK and moving bits, then LATCH, and finally a challenge: building a target pattern.
q58: First read the “What does this part do?” explanation and the circuit: three wires from the Arduino to pins 14, 11 and 12, and each output goes through a 220Ω resistor to an LED.
q59: Stage 1 — CLOCK: set DATA to 1 and give one CLOCK. Then set DATA to 0 and give CLOCK to watch that same 1 reach Q7 step by step.
q60: Stage 2 — LATCH: send in a few 1 bits and see that the LEDs are still off; then give LATCH so they all light at once.
q61: Stage 3 — challenge: send 8 bits so the LEDs match the “target” dots. The first bit you send ends up at Q7, so start the pattern from Q7.
